report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").


info.title: Exploring the effect of L1, linguistic, and non-linguistic variables on non-word repetition performance of monolingual and multilingual preschool children in Germany

text.text: Increasing linguistic diversity in society means that many children acquire the majority language as an additional language.

An important aspect of early language development is phonological processing, yet the factors underlying individual differences in monolingual and multilingual children in these abilities remain poorly understood.

To investigate these individual differences, the present study examined nonword repetition (NWR) performance in 793 children, including monolingual (n = 637) and multilingual (n = 156, 18 L1s) preschoolers (3-6 years) in Germany.

We used mixed-effects models to investigate the role of lexical linguistic distance to German, German exposure, receptive vocabulary, and morphological skills on NWR while controlling for child age, sex, cognitive ability, and parental education, with preschool as random intercepts Results showed an association of receptive vocabulary with NWR performance only.

These findings suggest that NWR performance in preschool children may be relatively independent of individual differences in linguistic background and exposure, while being moderately associated with lexical development.

In the context of a rise in global migration and the increase of linguistic diversity in societies, children as well as adults are faced with the need and challenge of learning a new or additional language.

For instance, in Germany, the proportion of population with an immigration background in 2025 was 31.1% (Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), 2026), and 42,7% were children under five in (Statistisches Bundesamt (Destatis), 2026).

text.text: The ASJP method computes distances between languages based on standardized lexical comparisons across a core vocabulary list.

The present study investigated individual differences in NWR performance in monolingual German-speaking and multilingual preschool children in Germany.

Overall, the findings suggest that LD and German language exposure did not show the hypothesized associations with NWR performance, while receptive vocabulary and expressive morphology were positively associated with NWR performance.

However, only receptive vocabulary retained its positive association in the full model, suggesting that lexical knowledge plays a particularly important and independent role in individual differences in NWR performance during the preschool period when other factors are controlled for.

Overall, the descriptive findings indicated small group differences in NWR performance between monolingual German-speaking and multilingual preschool children, which is in line with some previous findings (Core et al., 2017; Dos Santos & Ferré, 2018; Engel de Abreu, 2011; Lee et al., 2013; Meir & Armon-Lotem, 2017; Thordardottir & Brandeker, 2013).

text.text: It is important to interpret the absence of the LD effect precisely.

In the current study, LD captures overall phono-lexical similarity between languages but does not account for phonological complexity or structural differences between individual L1s and German phonological inventories.

Additionally, the results indicate that while LD does not affect NWR, it is associated with receptive vocabulary and expressive morphology, suggesting that the linguistic background has differential effects on specific language skills, providing further context for the unexpected positive LD association in the full model.
Likewise, exposure was not a significant predictor of NWR, which is in line with some previous findings (e.g., Engel et al., 2008; Meir & Armon-Lotem, 2017).

text.text: In the current study, exposure was measured by the time the children had spent in preschool, which does not capture qualitative aspects of input, such as the intensity or quality of German use during the day, nor does it include information about additional exposure to German outside preschool.

Consequently, the exposure variable does not fully reflect children's actual linguistic experience and may therefore have had limited validity and sensitivity in capturing the effect of language exposure on NWR performance.
In line with the third and fourth hypotheses, both receptive vocabulary and expressive morphology were positively associated with NWR performance in the univariate models.

This relationship is theoretically plausible, as a richer lexical inventory may support the formation and retention of phonological representations, thereby facilitating the repetition of novel sequences (Chiat, 2015; Gathercole, 2006; Lonigan et al., 2009).

The unexpected positive LD association may similarly reflect changes in the estimated relationships after controlling for other predictors, rather than an advantage of greater linguistic distance.
Receptive vocabulary retained its positive association in the sensitivity analysis excluding LD, supporting the consistency of this finding.
Nevertheless, the full model explained only a modest proportion of variance in NWR performance (R²m = .101; R²c = .126), leaving most individual differences unexplained by the variables examined.

text.text: The positive association between receptive vocabulary and NWR in the present study is consistent with these findings, suggesting that NWR performance, despite relatively small differences between monolingual and multilingual children, is not entirely independent of language-specific knowledge.

The present study shows that multilingual preschool children performed comparatively similarly to monolingual German-speaking children on NWR tasks despite substantially lower receptive vocabulary and expressive morphological skills.

In addition, lexical LD, German exposure, age, sex, and parental education showed no consistent association with NWR performance, whereas receptive vocabulary emerged as the strongest predictor of NWR.

Together, these findings suggest that phonological working memory, as assessed through NWR, may reflect cognitivephonological processing abilities that are comparatively less sensitive to multilingual language background and environmental factors during the preschool period than lexical and morphological language skills.
At the same time, the modest explanatory power of the full model indicates that substantial variability in NWR performance remained unexplained.

Future research should therefore further investigate the contribution of specific phonological characteristics of individual languages, qualitative aspects of language exposure, and additional cognitive mechanisms underlying phonological processing in multilingual children.
